chunks: What are 3D chips?. The question: What are 3D chips?
A 3D chip stacks several thin silicon dies on top of each other in one package and wires them together vertically.
Signals then travel tens of micrometers up instead of centimeters sideways. That gives huge bandwidth and uses less energy per bit.
The price is heat that is hard to remove, and more difficult testing.
Compare a sprawling town with a skyscraper. In the town, getting from one building to another means a long road. In the skyscraper, an elevator makes the trip in seconds.
Stacking dies is the skyscraper. The catch is heat: the lower floors must push their heat up through all the floors above, so the ground floor gets the warmest.
Connection count rises as 1/p².
Moving from a 40 µm microbump pitch to a 10 µm hybrid bond multiplies connection density by 16, which is what lets a cache die share a few thousand to tens of thousands of wires with the die below.
Die: one chip's worth of silicon. TSV (through-silicon via): a metal-filled vertical hole through a thinned die that carries signals and power to the die below or above.
Hybrid bonding: joining two dies face to face by bonding their copper pads directly, with no solder bumps. Bandwidth: how much data moves per second.
HBM (high bandwidth memory): a stack of memory dies with a very wide connection, placed next to a processor.
Take one HBM stack. It has 1024 separate vertical connections, and each carries 6. 4 Gb/s (billion bits per second). The total is 1024 times 6.
4 = 6,554 Gb/s, which is about 819 gigabytes per second (divide by 8 bits per byte).
To get that over a normal memory interface you would need dozens of channels and many more pins.
Wires matter too: crossing a die takes about 10 mm of wire, while a vertical hop is only about 0. 05 mm.
A short wire holds less charge that must be filled and emptied for every bit, so moving a bit costs far less energy. That is the whole idea.
"A 3D chip stacks active dies vertically and connects them with through-silicon vias or hybrid bonds, so signals travel tens of microns instead of centimetres.
That gives much higher bandwidth and lower energy per bit, which is how HBM and stacked cache work.
The trade-offs are heat, since lower dies must push heat through the others, plus harder power delivery, test and yield. 3D NAND is a related but different idea."
